title: Data drill: Greenleaf Pet Foods Ltd
intro: Read the case study first. Then choose which calculations are worth doing, work them out, and decide what the numbers show and where you would use them.
caseHtml:
Greenleaf Pet Foods Ltd

Greenleaf Pet Foods Ltd makes dry dog food from British ingredients. It sells to pet shops and online. In 2025 it ran its first national marketing campaign, using vets and dog trainers on social media.

The business is deciding whether to launch a premium range or a lower-priced range in 2026.

Table 1: UK dry dog food market
20242025
Market size£620m£682m
Table 2: Greenleaf, 2025
Revenue£15.5m
Marketing campaign spend£180,000
Estimated profit from the campaign£270,000

Premium dog food made up 22% of the market by value in 2025. A survey of 300 dog owners found 41% would pay more for food made from British ingredients (95% confidence interval: ±5.6 percentage points).

questions.text: Analyse one way in which the growth of the dry dog food market might affect Greenleaf’s revenue.
Assess whether Greenleaf’s 2025 marketing campaign was a success.
Greenleaf is choosing between launching a premium range or a lower-priced range in 2026. Evaluate these two options and recommend which it should choose.

calcs.why: Worth doing. The figure the question is built around.
calcs.formula: Change in market size ÷ original market size × 100

meaning.q: What does 10% market growth mean for Greenleaf?
opts: Greenleaf's sales could rise even without winning customers from rivals
Greenleaf's sales must have risen by 10%
meaning.why: A growing market brings new customers, but Greenleaf still has to win its share of them.

use.why: The figure the question is built around.

calcs.why: Worth doing. Puts Greenleaf's position in context for growth and for choosing a range.
calcs.formula: Sales of the business ÷ total sales in the market × 100

opts: Greenleaf is a small business in a big market, so even a small gain in share would add a lot of revenue
The market is too small for Greenleaf
meaning.why: A one percentage point gain in share would be worth about £6.8 million a year.

use.why: Puts Greenleaf's position in context for growth and for choosing a range.

calcs.why: Worth doing. This is the main evidence for judging the campaign.
calcs.formula: Profit from marketing activities ÷ marketing spend × 100

meaning.q: How should Greenleaf treat the 150% figure?
opts: It suggests the campaign paid for itself and more, but the profit is only an estimate
It proves the campaign caused all of the growth
meaning.why: Every £1 spent is estimated to have made £1.50 of profit. Some of those sales might have happened anyway because the market grew by 10%.

use.why: This is the main evidence for judging the campaign.

calcs.t: Size of the premium segment in 2025
calcs.why: Worth doing. Key data for choosing between the premium and lower-priced range.

meaning.q: What does the size of the premium segment tell Greenleaf?
opts: It is a large segment worth about £150 million, so a premium range would have plenty of potential customers
Most of the market is premium
The premium segment is too small to matter
Greenleaf already has most of the premium segment
meaning.why: About £150 million a year is spent on premium dog food. The survey suggests many owners might pay more for British ingredients, but it is only 300 people.

use.why: Key data for choosing between the premium and lower-priced range.

calcs.why: Greenleaf is a private limited company and the case gives no dividend or share data.
The confidence interval is already given (±5.6 percentage points). You use it to judge how reliable the 41% is; there is nothing to calculate.
